title: Chunking Strategies
summary: You can't embed a whole 50-page manual as one vector — retrieval needs small, self-contained units. Chunking splits documents into passages sized for both the embedding model and the answer. The choices — chunk size, overlap, and whether you split on fixed characters, recursively on structure, or by semantics — have an outsized effect on retrieval quality. You also attach metadata to each chunk so results can be filtered and cited. Get chunking wrong and even a perfect embedder retrieves garbage.

subtopics.title: Why chunk at all
subtopics.explanation: Embedding a huge document into one vector blurs many topics into a single point, so retrieval can't tell which part is relevant, and the passage is too long to paste into a prompt anyway. Splitting into focused chunks gives each a sharp, single-topic vector and a size the model can actually read. Chunking is therefore the bridge between raw documents and the per-passage retrieval RAG depends on.
subtopics.example:
doc = open("handbook.txt").read()   # 40,000 words

# BAD: one vector for the whole book -> meaning is averaged away
whole_vec = embed(doc)

# GOOD: many focused chunks, each about one thing
chunks = split(doc, size=800)
chunk_vecs = [embed(c) for c in chunks]
print(len(chunks))  # e.g. 260 retrievable units instead of 1 blur

subtopics.title: Chunk size and overlap
subtopics.explanation: Size sets how much context each chunk carries: too small loses meaning, too large dilutes the vector and wastes prompt budget. Overlap repeats a slice of text between adjacent chunks so a sentence split across a boundary still appears intact in one of them. Tuning size and overlap is the first knob that decides whether the answer's sentence survives inside a retrievable chunk.
subtopics.example:
def fixed_chunks(text, size=500, overlap=100):
    step = size - overlap          # advance less than size -> windows overlap
    chunks = []
    for start in range(0, len(text), step):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + size])
    return chunks

text = "a" * 1200
parts = fixed_chunks(text, size=500, overlap=100)
print([len(p) for p in parts])  # [500, 500, 300] -- overlapping windows

subtopics.title: Fixed vs recursive vs semantic
subtopics.explanation: Fixed splitting cuts every N characters and can slice mid-sentence; recursive splitting tries natural separators in order (paragraphs, then lines, then sentences) so chunks respect structure; semantic splitting groups sentences by embedding similarity so each chunk is one coherent idea. Recursive is the pragmatic default, semantic is best-quality-costliest. Choosing the splitter is choosing how faithfully your chunks preserve the document's meaning.

subtopics.title: Attaching metadata
subtopics.explanation: Each chunk should travel with metadata — source file, title, page or section, and a stable id — stored alongside its vector. That metadata lets you filter retrieval (only this product's docs), cite the exact source in the answer, and debug which chunk produced a claim. Metadata is what turns a bare vector into a citable, filterable retrieval unit.

subtopics.title: Chunking's outsized effect on quality
subtopics.explanation: No embedder can retrieve an answer that was split away or buried in an off-topic mega-chunk, so poor chunking silently caps the ceiling of the whole RAG system regardless of model quality. Small changes to size, overlap, and splitter often move end-to-end accuracy more than swapping the embedding model. That leverage is why chunking is tuned early and evaluated deliberately rather than picked by default.
subtopics.example:
# Same docs + same embedder, only chunking changed:
# size=2000, overlap=0   -> answer sentence buried in a 4-topic chunk
# size=400,  overlap=80  -> answer sentence isolated + intact
# Measured on a QA set:
scores = {"big_no_overlap": 0.58, "tuned": 0.81}
print(scores)  # chunking alone moved accuracy 23 points

foundations.overview: Retrieval operates on passages, not whole documents, so before anything can be embedded or searched a document must be split into chunks. Chunking is deceptively high-leverage: embedding a whole file into one vector averages away its many topics and produces a blur no retriever can use, while chunks that are too small lose the surrounding context needed to understand them. The core knobs are chunk size and overlap — overlap repeats a slice of text across adjacent chunks so a sentence straddling a boundary still lands intact somewhere. The splitting strategy matters just as much: fixed-length cuts every N characters and can slice mid-sentence; recursive splitting prefers natural separators (paragraph, line, sentence) so chunks respect structure and is the pragmatic default; semantic splitting groups sentences by embedding similarity for the most coherent chunks at higher cost. Every chunk should carry metadata — source, title, section, stable id — enabling filtered retrieval and citations. Because no embedder can retrieve an answer that chunking destroyed or buried, tuning size, overlap, and splitter often moves end-to-end accuracy more than changing the model itself.
foundations.formalDefinition: Chunking is the preprocessing step that partitions a document into a sequence of text segments (chunks), typically bounded by a target size with optional overlap, using a splitting strategy (fixed-length, recursive by separator hierarchy, or semantic by embedding similarity), and annotates each chunk with metadata for filtering and citation prior to embedding and indexing.
foundations.whyItMatters: Chunking sets the ceiling on retrieval quality: an answer split across a boundary or buried in an off-topic mega-chunk can never be retrieved cleanly no matter how good the embedder is. It is one of the cheapest, highest-impact levers in a RAG pipeline and a common root cause of 'RAG doesn't work' failures.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of chunking as deciding the size of index cards you'll file in a card catalog. Cards too big and each mixes many unrelated notes so you can't find one fact; too small and a single idea gets torn across cards; overlap is copying the last line of one card onto the next so a sentence spanning two cards survives. Recursive splitting is cutting along the document's natural seams instead of with a paper cutter at fixed intervals.
foundations.performanceImpact: Smaller chunks mean more vectors to store and search (larger index, more query cost) but sharper relevance; larger chunks shrink the index but risk diluting vectors and blowing the prompt budget. Overlap multiplies chunk count by roughly size/(size-overlap), so heavy overlap noticeably increases storage and embedding cost.
commonUseCases: Splitting PDFs, wikis, and manuals into retrievable passages
Recursive splitting to respect paragraph/section structure
Attaching source/section metadata for filtering and citation

commonMisconceptions.myth: Bigger chunks are safer because they contain more context.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Large chunks dilute the embedding across many topics and waste prompt budget, often lowering retrieval precision. There's a sweet spot; bigger is not automatically better.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Overlap is wasteful and should be zero.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Zero overlap frequently splits the answer sentence across a boundary so it appears fully in no chunk. Modest overlap (10-20% of size) is a cheap insurance against boundary loss.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Chunking is a solved detail; only the embedder matters.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Chunking commonly moves end-to-end accuracy more than the embedding model does. A great embedder cannot retrieve an answer that bad chunking destroyed.

interactiveExamples.title: Fixed-size chunking with overlap
interactiveExamples.explanation: A minimal character-based chunker that slides a window of a given size, advancing by size minus overlap so adjacent chunks share text. See how overlap keeps a boundary-spanning sentence intact in at least one chunk.

code.code:
def fixed_chunks(text, size=200, overlap=40):
    step = size - overlap
    chunks = []
    for start in range(0, len(text), step):
        chunk = text[start:start + size]
        if chunk.strip():
            chunks.append(chunk)
    return chunks

doc = ("Refunds are processed within 14 days. "
       "Enterprise accounts are prorated. "
       "Contact billing for exceptions.")
chunks = fixed_chunks(doc, size=60, overlap=20)
for i, c in enumerate(chunks):
    print(i, repr(c))
print("num_chunks:", len(chunks))
code.caption: Each window is 60 chars and starts 40 chars after the previous, so 20 chars overlap — a sentence split at char 60 still appears whole in the next chunk.
code.expectedOutput:
0 'Refunds are processed within 14 days. Enterprise accounts ar'
1 'terprise accounts are prorated. Contact billing for exceptio'
2 'billing for exceptions.'
num_chunks: 3

interactiveExamples.explanation: A recursive splitter tries coarse separators (blank line, newline, sentence) before falling back to finer ones, keeping chunks under a size limit while respecting structure. Each resulting chunk is wrapped in a record with a stable id and source metadata, ready to embed and index.

code.caption: The splitter breaks on the blank line first, then sentences, keeping each chunk under 40 chars and tagging it with a citable id and source.

codeLab.title: Build a sentence-aware chunker with overlap
codeLab.instructions: Implement chunk_sentences(text: str, max_chars: int, overlap_sentences: int) -> list[str]. Split text into sentences on '. ' (keep it simple; assume sentences end with a period and a space), then greedily pack whole sentences into chunks so each chunk's length stays <= max_chars. When you start a new chunk, prepend the last `overlap_sentences` sentences from the previous chunk so context carries over. Never split a sentence across chunks, and skip empty results. Complete the function so the harness passes.

starter.code:

    # Split into sentences on '. ' (re-add the period), then greedily pack
    # whole sentences into chunks <= max_chars, carrying `overlap_sentences`
    # sentences from the end of one chunk into the start of the next.
    # TODO: implement
    ...

solution.code:
def chunk_sentences(text: str, max_chars: int, overlap_sentences: int) -> list[str]:
    # split into sentences, re-attaching the period so each is self-contained
    raw = [s.strip() for s in text.split(". ") if s.strip()]
    sentences = [s if s.endswith(".") else s + "." for s in raw]

    chunks = []
    current = []          # list of sentences in the chunk being built
    for sent in sentences:
        candidate = current + [sent]
        if len(" ".join(candidate)) <= max_chars or not current:
            current = candidate
        else:
            chunks.append(" ".join(current))
            # carry the last `overlap_sentences` sentences into the new chunk
            carry = current[-overlap_sentences:] if overlap_sentences else []
            current = carry + [sent]
    if current:
        chunks.append(" ".join(current))
    return [c for c in chunks if c.strip()]

codeLab.testHarness:
def sentences_of(chunk):
    return {s.strip().rstrip('.') for s in chunk.split('. ') if s.strip()}

text = ('Refunds take 14 days. Enterprise is prorated. '
        'Contact billing for help. No exceptions apply.')
chunks = chunk_sentences(text, max_chars=45, overlap_sentences=1)

# more than one chunk was produced
assert len(chunks) >= 2, chunks
# sentences are never cut mid-way (every chunk ends with a period)
assert all(c.endswith('.') for c in chunks), chunks
# overlap: some sentence appears in two adjacent chunks
assert any(
    sentences_of(chunks[i]) & sentences_of(chunks[i + 1])
    for i in range(len(chunks) - 1)
), 'expected overlapping sentences'
# a lone sentence that fits stays in its own chunk (no over-splitting)
assert chunk_sentences('Only one sentence here.', max_chars=100, overlap_sentences=1) == ['Only one sentence here.']
print('all tests passed')
hints: Split on '. ' but re-add a trailing '.' to each sentence so chunks read cleanly and end on a period.
Greedily append whole sentences while the joined length stays under max_chars; start a new chunk when the next sentence would overflow.
For overlap, seed the new chunk with current[-overlap_sentences:] before adding the overflowing sentence.

debuggingLab.title: Zero overlap split the answer in half
debuggingLab.scenario: Your RAG bot can't answer 'what is the enterprise refund window?' even though the fact is in the docs. The culprit is the chunker: it uses fixed-size slicing with no overlap, and the sentence 'Enterprise refunds are processed within 14 days' happens to fall exactly on a chunk boundary — the words 'within 14 days' end up in a different chunk from 'Enterprise refunds', so neither chunk embeds as a good match for the query and the answer is never retrieved intact.

buggyCode.code:
def chunk(text, size=40):
    # no overlap: adjacent chunks share nothing
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), size)]

doc = "Enterprise refunds are processed within 14 days per policy."
chunks = chunk(doc, size=40)
for c in chunks:
    print(repr(c))
# 'Enterprise refunds are processed within '  <- has the subject
# '14 days per policy.'                        <- has the number
# the answer '14 days' is separated from 'Enterprise refunds'

debuggingLab.diagnosis: Fixed slicing with step == size means chunk boundaries fall at arbitrary character positions with no shared text between neighbors. When a key sentence straddles a boundary, its subject lands in one chunk and its answer value in another. Each partial chunk embeds poorly against the query, so retrieval either misses it or returns a fragment that lacks the full fact. The root cause is not the embedder — it's that no single chunk ever contained the complete answer sentence.
debuggingLab.lesson: Boundary loss is one of the most common silent RAG bugs. Fixed-size chunking with zero overlap will eventually cut an answer in half; adding modest overlap (roughly 10-25% of chunk size) guarantees any sentence spanning a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk. Better still, split on natural separators (recursive splitting) so boundaries fall between sentences rather than through them.
debuggingLab.expectedOutput:
'Enterprise refunds are processed within '
'ocessed within 14 days per policy.'
'r policy.'

productionDeepDive.architecture: Make chunking an explicit, versioned pipeline stage: loader -> cleaner -> splitter -> metadata enricher -> embedder -> index writer. Keep the splitter behind one interface so you can swap fixed/recursive/semantic strategies without touching the rest, and store the chunking config (size, overlap, strategy, version) alongside the index so you know how any vector was produced. Each chunk record carries a stable id, its text, and metadata (source, section, offsets) for citation and re-indexing.
productionDeepDive.performance: Chunk count drives both embedding cost at index time and query cost at search time, and overlap multiplies count by roughly size/(size-overlap). Batch embedding calls, cache embeddings keyed by a hash of chunk text + model so unchanged chunks are never re-embedded, and pick the largest chunk size that still retrieves precisely to keep the index small.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Handle real-world documents defensively: strip boilerplate and control characters, normalize whitespace, and guard against a single 'sentence' larger than max_chars by hard-splitting it as a last resort so the splitter never emits an oversized chunk or loops. Make re-indexing idempotent via stable ids so re-ingesting a document updates rather than duplicates chunks.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log the chunk-size distribution, count, and overlap ratio per document, and track retrieval-hit rate per chunking version on an eval question set. A sudden shift in average chunk size or a drop in hit rate after a config change surfaces a chunking regression before users notice missing answers.
productionDeepDive.security: Chunk metadata must carry access-control tags (tenant, permission scope) so retrieval can filter by the requesting user's rights — otherwise a shared index can leak one customer's chunk to another. Sanitize document text during chunking to strip embedded instructions that could later become prompt-injection payloads when a chunk is pasted into the generator.
productionDeepDive.cost: The dominant levers are chunk count and re-embedding. Right-size chunks and overlap so you store the fewest vectors that still answer well, and use content-hash caching so a document edit re-embeds only changed chunks. Semantic chunking improves quality but adds embedding calls during splitting, so reserve it for corpora where coherence measurably lifts accuracy.

caseStudies.company: A SaaS company building a docs assistant
caseStudies.problem: Their RAG assistant frequently answered 'I don't know' for facts that were clearly in the documentation. Investigation showed a fixed 1000-character splitter with zero overlap was slicing answer sentences across chunk boundaries and merging unrelated sections into single blurry vectors.
caseStudies.solution: They switched to recursive splitting on paragraph/sentence separators with a 600-character target and 15% overlap, attached section-title metadata to every chunk, and added an eval set to measure retrieval-hit rate per chunking version before shipping.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: The smaller, overlapping chunks roughly doubled the vector count, increasing storage and per-query search cost, and semantic-aware splitting added ingestion time; in exchange retrieval-hit rate rose sharply and 'I don't know' responses dropped substantially.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat chunking as a first-class, evaluated pipeline stage — tune size, overlap, and splitter against a QA set — because it often moves end-to-end accuracy more than swapping the embedding model.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do we chunk documents instead of embedding each whole file as one vector?
options: Embedding models reject long inputs entirely
A single vector averages many topics into a blur retrieval can't localize, and the text is too long to prompt with
It makes the index larger, which is always better
checkpoints.explanation: One vector for a whole document mixes all its topics into a single point, so retrieval can't tell which part is relevant, and the passage is too long to paste into a prompt. Focused chunks give sharp, single-topic vectors.

checkpoints.prompt: This chunker is meant to overlap adjacent windows but doesn't. What's wrong?
options: step must be size - overlap, so windows advance less than their width and actually overlap
checkpoints.explanation: With step == size, each window starts exactly where the last ended, so there is no shared text. Overlap requires step = size - overlap so consecutive windows share `overlap` characters.

theory.question: Why is chunk overlap important, and how do you choose the overlap amount?
theory.directAnswer: Overlap repeats a slice of text between adjacent chunks so a sentence or fact that straddles a chunk boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk, which keeps it retrievable. You typically set overlap to roughly 10-25% of chunk size — enough to bridge boundaries without exploding the chunk count.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Overlap is the number of characters or sentences shared between the end of one chunk and the start of the next.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Fixed boundaries inevitably cut some sentences in half, splitting a subject from its value so neither partial chunk embeds well against a query; overlap ensures the whole fact lives in one chunk.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The splitter advances by size minus overlap (or carries the last N sentences into the next chunk), so consecutive chunks share text; the chunk count grows by about size/(size - overlap).

theory.whyImportant: Boundary loss is a leading cause of 'the answer is in the docs but the bot can't find it', and overlap is the cheapest fix.
theory.realWorldExample: A refund policy sentence split across two zero-overlap chunks was never retrieved; adding 15% overlap put the full sentence in one chunk and restored the answer.

followUps.question: What's the cost of too much overlap?
followUps.answer: It multiplies chunk count, increasing embedding and storage cost and search latency, with diminishing quality gains; 10-25% is a common sweet spot.

followUps.question: Can you avoid the boundary problem another way?
followUps.answer: Yes — split on natural separators (recursive or semantic splitting) so boundaries fall between sentences rather than through them, reducing reliance on overlap.

theory.question: Compare fixed-size, recursive, and semantic chunking. When would you use each?
theory.directAnswer: Fixed-size cuts every N characters — simplest and fastest but can slice mid-sentence. Recursive splits on a hierarchy of natural separators (paragraph, line, sentence) so chunks respect structure; it's the pragmatic default. Semantic groups sentences by embedding similarity so each chunk is one coherent idea — highest quality but costliest, since it embeds during splitting.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three strategies for deciding where to place chunk boundaries: by fixed length, by separator hierarchy, or by meaning.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Documents have structure and meaning that fixed cuts ignore; recursive and semantic splitting preserve more of it, trading compute for boundary quality.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Fixed uses a sliding window; recursive tries coarse separators first and falls back to finer ones to stay under a size limit; semantic embeds sentences and starts a new chunk when similarity to the running group drops below a threshold.

theory.whyImportant: Boundary placement directly affects whether a whole fact lands in one chunk, so the strategy choice is a major retrieval-quality lever.
theory.realWorldExample: For a structured handbook, recursive splitting on headings and paragraphs gave clean, citable chunks; a narrative report with no clear structure benefited from semantic chunking to keep each idea together.

followUps.question: Why not always use semantic chunking?
followUps.answer: It requires embedding sentences during ingestion, adding cost and latency; reserve it for corpora where coherence measurably lifts accuracy.

followUps.question: What's a good default?
followUps.answer: Recursive splitting with a moderate size and 10-20% overlap handles most structured documents well and is cheap.

scenario.question: Users report the RAG bot says 'I don't know' for facts that are definitely in the docs. How do you diagnose and fix it, focusing on chunking?
scenario.directAnswer: Reproduce a failing query, inspect the retrieved chunks, and check whether the answer sentence is intact in any chunk. If it's split across boundaries or buried in an oversized multi-topic chunk, fix chunking: switch to recursive splitting, right-size chunks, add 10-20% overlap, and attach section metadata; then measure retrieval-hit rate on an eval set before and after.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A retrieval-recall failure whose root cause is upstream in the chunking stage rather than the embedder or generator.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Zero-overlap fixed splitting slices answer sentences across boundaries, and oversized chunks dilute vectors so the right passage never ranks high enough to be retrieved.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Log what retrieval actually returned for the failing query, confirm the full fact isn't in any single chunk, adjust size/overlap/strategy, re-index, and verify hit-rate improves on held-out questions.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows debugging RAG end-to-end and recognizing that 'the model is bad' is often really 'chunking hid the answer', the cheapest place to fix.
scenario.realWorldExample: Retrieved chunks showed the refund window split from its subject; moving to recursive splitting with overlap and section metadata raised hit-rate sharply and eliminated most 'I don't know' answers.

followUps.question: How do you know it's chunking and not the embedder?
followUps.answer: Inspect the retrieved chunks: if no single chunk contains the full answer, it's a chunking problem; if the right chunk exists but ranks low, look at the embedder or hybrid search.

followUps.question: How do you prevent regressions?
followUps.answer: Version the chunking config, keep an eval question set, and track retrieval-hit rate per version so a config change that hurts recall is caught before release.

coding.question: Write a fixed-size character chunker with overlap that never emits empty chunks and returns each chunk with a stable id and its start offset in metadata.
coding.thoughtProcess: I advance the window by size minus overlap so neighbors share text, slice the window, skip blanks, and for each kept chunk build a record with a deterministic id (source + running index) and the start offset so callers can cite and re-index. Guarding overlap < size prevents a non-advancing (infinite) loop.
lineByLine: Guard that overlap < size so step is positive and the loop always advances, preventing an infinite loop.
step = size - overlap makes consecutive windows share `overlap` characters.
range(0, len(text), step) yields each window's start offset.
Blank/whitespace-only slices are skipped so no empty chunk is emitted.
Each kept chunk gets a deterministic id (source + running index) and records its start offset for citation and idempotent re-indexing.
The __main__ block prints ids, offsets, and text so overlapping windows are visible.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the text length; each character is copied into a constant number of overlapping windows.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the emitted chunk text (slightly more than n due to overlap).

followUps.question: How would you make re-indexing idempotent?
followUps.answer: Use stable ids derived from source plus index (or a content hash) so re-ingesting a document updates existing records instead of creating duplicates.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to respect sentence boundaries?
followUps.answer: Replace fixed slicing with recursive splitting on separators, greedily packing whole sentences under the size limit while still carrying overlap sentences between chunks.

keyTakeaways: Chunking splits documents into small, self-contained passages so each gets a sharp, single-topic vector that fits a prompt.
Chunk size and overlap are the primary knobs: modest overlap (10-25%) keeps boundary-spanning sentences intact in at least one chunk.
Recursive splitting on natural separators is the pragmatic default; semantic splitting is best-quality but costliest; fixed slicing is simplest but can cut sentences.
Attach metadata (source, section, stable id) to every chunk to enable filtered retrieval, citations, and idempotent re-indexing.
Chunking sets the ceiling on retrieval quality — tuning it against an eval set often moves accuracy more than swapping the embedding model.
